narr: Welcome to weeks five through seven of Linear Algebra I. We'll explore matrix operations, special matrices, inverses, and decomposition methods.
Let's start with an explicit example of non-commutativity.

data.heading: Example 1 — Non-commutativity of matrices
data.problem: Given matrices A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, find AB and BA.

narr: Let's consider two simple matrices A and B.
When we multiply A by B, we get this result.
But when we multiply B by A, we get a different result.
This shows that matrix multiplication is non-commutative - the order matters.

data.title: 3.5.3 Special matrices and elimination matrices
data.subtitle: Identity, diagonal, triangular matrices and elimination

narr: Now let's explore special types of matrices and elimination matrices.
The identity matrix leaves vectors unchanged.
Diagonal matrices scale coordinates.
Upper triangular matrices have zeros below the diagonal.
Lower triangular matrices have zeros above the diagonal.

data.heading: Special matrix types
bullets: Identity matrix I: leaves vectors unchanged
Diagonal D = diag(d₁, ..., dₙ): scales coordinates
Upper triangular: zeros below the diagonal
Lower triangular: zeros above the diagonal
Triangular systems: solved by forward/backward substitution

narr: The identity matrix is special because it doesn't change vectors at all.
Diagonal matrices simply scale each coordinate by a different factor.
Upper triangular matrices have all zeros below the main diagonal.
Lower triangular matrices have all zeros above the main diagonal.
Solving systems with triangular matrices is efficient using forward or backward substitution.

data.heading: Example 2 — Elimination matrix
data.problem: Show how the elimination operation R₂ ← R₂ - 3R₁ corresponds to matrix multiplication.
steps: The elimination operation is represented by matrix E = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Multiply E by the original matrix: E · \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 6 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
The inverse of E is E⁻¹ = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, which restores the original rows
data.result: The transformed system is EAx = Eb, and E⁻¹ restores the original rows.

narr: Elimination operations can be represented as matrix multiplication.
The operation R₂ ← R₂ - 3R₁ corresponds to multiplying by this matrix E.
When we apply E to our original matrix, we get the transformed matrix.
The inverse of E allows us to restore the original rows.

data.title: 3.5.4 The inverse matrix: definition, criteria, rules
data.subtitle: Understanding matrix inverses

narr: Let's dive deeper into inverse matrices.
The inverse of a matrix reverses its linear transformation.
For a matrix A, its inverse A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I.
This means that if Ax = b, then x = A⁻¹b for any b.

data.heading: Inverse matrix properties
bullets: AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I
If Ax = 0 for nonzero x, the inverse does not exist
For a square A, these are equivalent: inverse exists ⇔ all pivots nonzero ⇔ columns independent ⇔ Ax = 0 only when x = 0 ⇔ Ax = b has unique solution for any b
(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹
(Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ
(A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A
(Aᵏ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵏ

narr: The inverse matrix satisfies this fundamental property.
If a matrix maps a nonzero vector to zero, it can't have an inverse.
For square matrices, several conditions are equivalent to having an inverse.
The order of factors in the inverse of a product is reversed.
The inverse of a transpose is the transpose of the inverse.
The inverse of an inverse is the original matrix.
The inverse of a power is the power of the inverse.

data.title: 3.5.5 The inverse of 2 × 2 and the Gauss-Jordan method
data.subtitle: Computing inverses for 2×2 matrices and beyond

narr: Let's look at how to compute inverses specifically for 2×2 matrices.
We'll also explore the Gauss-Jordan method for finding inverses.

data.heading: Inverse of a 2×2 matrix
data.tex: \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}

narr: For a 2×2 matrix, the inverse can be computed directly using this formula.
The denominator is the determinant of the matrix.
If the determinant is zero, the matrix doesn't have an inverse.
Let's find the inverse of this specific 2×2 matrix.
First, we compute its determinant, which happens to be 1.
Then we apply the inverse formula to get our result.

data.heading: Example 4 — Gauss-Jordan method
data.problem: Find the inverse of \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7 \end{pmatrix} using Gauss-Jordan elimination

narr: For larger matrices, we can use the Gauss-Jordan method.
We start with the augmented matrix [A|I].
Then we apply row operations to transform A into I.
When we're done, I will have been transformed into A⁻¹.
This method works for any size matrix, not just 2×2.

data.heading: Columns of the inverse matrix
bullets: If A⁻¹ = [x₁ ... xₙ], then Axⱼ = eⱼ
Finding the inverse means solving n systems
For a single system Ax = b, triangular elimination is usually preferable to explicit computation of A⁻¹

narr: The columns of the inverse matrix have an interesting interpretation.
Each column xⱼ of A⁻¹ satisfies Axⱼ = eⱼ, where eⱼ is the j-th standard basis vector.
This means finding the inverse is equivalent to solving n different systems.
For solving a single system Ax = b, it's often better to use triangular elimination rather than computing the full inverse.

data.title: 3.5.6 LU decomposition and solving systems through factors
data.subtitle: Factorizing matrices into lower and upper triangular matrices

narr: Now let's explore LU decomposition, which factorizes a matrix into lower and upper triangular matrices.
This approach is efficient for solving systems with multiple right-hand sides.

data.heading: LU decomposition
bullets: A = LU: elimination factors
L is unit lower triangular (1s on diagonal)
U is upper triangular
Ek · · · E₂E₁A = U → A = E₁⁻¹E₂⁻¹ · · · Ek⁻¹U = LU
Solving: first Ly = b by forward substitution, then Ux = y by backward substitution

narr: LU decomposition factorizes a matrix A into L and U.
L is a unit lower triangular matrix with 1s on the diagonal.
U is an upper triangular matrix.
The elimination matrices E₁, E₂, etc., combine to form L.
To solve Ax = b, we first solve Ly = b, then Ux = y.

data.heading: Example 5 — LU decomposition
steps: The inverse of E is L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
The upper triangular matrix is U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
data.result: A = LU where L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}

narr: Let's find the LU decomposition of this matrix.
First, we perform elimination to get the upper triangular matrix U.
The elimination operation corresponds to matrix E.
The inverse of E gives us L.
We verify that LU equals our original matrix A.

data.heading: Example 6 — Solving with LU decomposition
data.problem: Solve Ax = b where A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 6 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, b = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 19 \end{pmatrix}
steps: Use LU decomposition: A = LU where L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
First solve Ly = b: \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} y₁ \\ y₂ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 19 \end{pmatrix}
Then solve Ux = y: \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x₁ \\ x₂ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}

narr: Once we have the LU decomposition, solving systems becomes efficient.
We first solve Ly = b using forward substitution.
Then we solve Ux = y using backward substitution.
This approach is particularly useful when we need to solve multiple systems with the same matrix A but different right-hand sides.

data.title: 3.5.7 LDU decomposition, pivots and determinant
data.subtitle: Refining LU decomposition and connecting to determinants

narr: Let's refine our LU decomposition to LDU form and connect it to pivots and determinants.

data.heading: LDU decomposition
bullets: U = D · (D⁻¹U), where D contains reference elements of U
A = L · D · (D⁻¹U) with unit diagonals for L and D⁻¹U
Example: \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 6 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} · \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} · \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}

narr: LDU decomposition further refines LU by factoring out the diagonal.
D contains the diagonal elements of U.
This gives us matrices with unit diagonals for L and D⁻¹U.

data.heading: Pivots and determinant
data.tex: For A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} with a ≠ 0, the pivots are a and d - cb/a, and their product is ad - bc = det A

narr: The pivots are important in understanding the matrix.
For a 2×2 matrix, the first pivot is simply the top-left element.
The second pivot is adjusted based on the elimination.
The product of the pivots equals the determinant of the matrix.

data.heading: Determinant properties
bullets: Without row exchanges, det(A) equals the product of pivots
The normalized LDU is unique when it exists with nonzero pivots

narr: When no row exchanges are needed, the determinant is simply the product of the pivots.
The normalized LDU decomposition is unique when it exists with nonzero pivots.

data.title: 3.5.8 Permutations, PA = LU and partial pivoting
data.subtitle: Handling zero pivots with row exchanges

narr: Sometimes we encounter zero pivots, which can be handled through row exchanges.
Let's explore how permutation matrices help with this.

data.heading: Permutation matrices
bullets: Permutation matrices permute rows of I
There is exactly one 1 in each row and each column
Example: P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} exchanges rows
P⁻¹ = Pᵀ (since Pᵀ · P = I)

narr: Permutation matrices are formed by rearranging the rows of the identity matrix.
Each permutation matrix has exactly one 1 in each row and column.
For example, this matrix swaps the two rows of a matrix it multiplies.
The inverse of a permutation matrix is its transpose.

data.heading: Example 7 — PA = LU decomposition
steps: Since the first pivot is zero, we need to exchange rows
Now we have PA = LU where L = I and U = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
data.result: PA = LU where P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, U = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}

narr: When we encounter a zero pivot, we can exchange rows to proceed.
This is done using a permutation matrix P.
Multiplying by P exchanges the rows of A.
Now we can perform LU decomposition on PA instead of A.

data.heading: Partial pivoting
bullets: Rule: take the largest in magnitude element of the active column
Avoids multipliers that are too large
Example: for \begin{pmatrix} 10^{-8} & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, exchanging rows avoids a multiplier of 10^8

narr: Partial pivoting is a strategy to improve numerical stability.
The rule is to select the largest element in magnitude in the current column as the pivot.
This helps avoid large multipliers that can amplify rounding errors.
In this example, exchanging rows prevents an extremely large multiplier.

data.title: 3.5.9 Transposition, symmetric matrices, LDLᵀ
data.subtitle: Working with transposes and symmetric matrices

narr: Let's explore matrix transposition and symmetric matrices.
We'll also look at the special LDLᵀ decomposition for symmetric matrices.

data.heading: Matrix transposition
bullets: (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ
(A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ
(AB)ᵀ = Bᵀ · Aᵀ

narr: The transpose of a matrix flips its rows and columns.
The transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes.
The transpose of a product reverses the order of multiplication.
Let's see how to compute the transpose of a matrix.
We simply flip the rows and columns.
The element at position (i,j) in the transpose comes from position (j,i) in the original.

data.heading: Symmetric matrices and LDLᵀ decomposition
bullets: A symmetric matrix satisfies Aᵀ = A
If a symmetric A has an LDU decomposition without exchanges, its normalized upper factor equals Lᵀ: A = LDLᵀ
Example: \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} · \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} · \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}

narr: A symmetric matrix is equal to its own transpose.
For symmetric matrices, we can use a special LDLᵀ decomposition.
This is similar to LDU but with the upper triangular matrix being the transpose of L.
Let's explore some practical applications of matrix decompositions.
We'll look at difference matrices, sum matrices, and tridiagonal systems.

data.heading: Difference matrix
bullets: A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Ax = (x₁, x₂ - x₁, x₃ - x₂)ᵀ
Its inverse A⁻¹ = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} gives cumulative sums
This is the discrete analog of differentiation and integration

narr: The difference matrix computes discrete differences between consecutive elements.
When applied to a vector x, it gives the differences between consecutive elements.
Its inverse computes cumulative sums, which is like integration.
Together, they represent discrete differentiation and integration.

data.heading: Tridiagonal systems
bullets: A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Describes nearest neighbor connections (finite difference equations)
Its factors preserve the narrow band
Solving via LU uses the structure, avoiding the dense inverse matrix

narr: Tridiagonal matrices have nonzero elements only on the main diagonal and adjacent diagonals.
They often arise in problems involving nearest neighbor connections.
When solving systems with tridiagonal matrices, LU decomposition preserves the structure.
This is more efficient than computing the full inverse matrix.
Let's summarize the key concepts we've covered in weeks five through seven.
Matrix multiplication is non-commutative - the order matters.
We explored various special matrices including identity, diagonal, and triangular matrices.
Inverse matrices reverse linear transformations and have specific properties.
LU and LDU decompositions help solve systems efficiently.
Permutation matrices handle zero pivots through row exchanges.
Symmetric matrices have special properties and decompositions.
Finally, we saw practical applications in difference matrices and tridiagonal systems.
